posts.title: Claude Code persistent memory changes the loop
posts.hook: Claude Code remembering context across sessions quietly changed how I build.
posts.body:
Claude Code remembering context across sessions quietly changed how I build.

Before persistent memory, every session started with me re-explaining the repo structure, the naming conventions, which files matter, what we tried last time that didn't work.

Now I open a terminal and it already knows:
- The project uses SQLite, not Postgres
- We tried Playwright for that scraper and it broke on auth
- The webhook format changed last Tuesday
- Which voice rules to follow when drafting content

It sounds small. It's not. The re-orientation tax on every session was 5-10 minutes of context loading before any real work happened. Multiply that across 15-20 sessions a day and you're burning over an hour just getting the agent back to where you left off.

The bigger shift is what it does to trust. When the agent remembers your past mistakes and doesn't repeat them, you start delegating harder tasks. You stop babysitting. You let it run.

I wrote a CLAUDE.md and a lessons.md months ago to simulate this manually. Now the model just... does it. The manual scaffolding still helps, but the gap between "agent with amnesia" and "agent with memory" is the gap between a contractor and a teammate.
posts.cta: If you're building with coding agents daily, how are you handling session continuity?

remixes.hook: The best coding agent session isn't the first one. It's the 30th.
remixes.body:
The best coding agent session isn't the first one. It's the 30th.

Session 1, you're explaining everything. File structure. Naming conventions. Why you chose SQLite over Postgres. Which approach failed last Tuesday.

Session 30, you open a terminal and say "add the webhook retry logic we talked about" and it just does it. No preamble. No re-onboarding. It remembers the failed Playwright scraper. It knows your test runner quirks. It knows which config files it shouldn't touch.

This is what persistent memory in Claude Code actually unlocked for me. Not a feature checkbox. A compounding relationship with a tool.

Every session deposits context. Every future session withdraws from it. The ROI curve bends upward the longer you stick with one agent on one codebase.

Most people evaluate coding agents on a single session. That's like judging a hire after one day. The real value shows up when the tool stops needing you to babysit it.

I've watched my setup time per session drop from 10 minutes of context-setting to basically zero. That's not a marginal improvement. That's a different workflow entirely.

Every AI coding session used to start with an onboarding tax. I stopped paying it.

The tax looked like this: paste in the README. Explain the folder layout. Remind the model which ORM you use. Re-describe the bug you were halfway through fixing yesterday. Copy in the error log from the last attempt.

15 minutes of setup before any real work happened. Every single time.

Claude Code's persistent memory files eliminated that entire ritual. I have a MEMORY.md that accumulates project knowledge across sessions. Architecture decisions, file paths, things that broke and why, user preferences.

The shift is subtle but massive. Instead of "let me explain my project to you," it's "pick up where we left off." The agent already knows the codebase uses launchd not cron. Already knows the pre-push hook runs a blocklist scan. Already knows we tried approach A and it failed on auth.

This isn't about the AI being smarter. It's about not throwing away context every time you close a terminal.

The developers getting the most leverage right now aren't the ones with the fanciest prompts. They're the ones who stopped re-explaining their codebase every morning.

posts.title: LLM bills are the new cloud bills
posts.hook: Most teams don't have an LLM cost problem. They have a routing problem.
posts.body:
Most teams don't have an LLM cost problem. They have a routing problem.

I've seen teams running Opus on tasks that Haiku handles fine. Sending 200k token contexts when 20k would do. Calling the API synchronously when they could batch. No caching layer. No model tiering.

The fix isn't switching to a cheaper model. It's building a routing layer that matches task complexity to model capability.

What that looks like in practice:

1. Classification tasks, extraction, formatting... Haiku. Costs nearly nothing.
2. Content drafting, analysis, code review... Sonnet. Good enough 90% of the time.
3. Architecture decisions, complex reasoning, novel problems... Opus. Worth every token.

Add prompt caching on repeated system prompts and you cut another 30-40% off the bill without touching output quality.

The teams spending $140k/month on inference aren't using better AI. They're using expensive AI on cheap problems. That's not an AI strategy, it's a missing if-statement.

I run three different models across my stack for exactly this reason. Claude Code gets Opus because the reasoning matters. My chat agent runs Sonnet because conversational responses don't need frontier reasoning. Batch jobs get Haiku.

Same quality. Fraction of the cost.

remixes.label: model-tiering-playbook
remixes.hook: I cut our LLM spend by 60% without changing a single prompt.
remixes.body:
I cut our LLM spend by 60% without changing a single prompt.

The move was embarrassingly simple: stop sending every request to the same model.

Here's what the routing layer looks like in practice. Classification tasks, data extraction, simple formatting? Haiku. Costs nearly nothing and handles it perfectly. Complex reasoning, multi-step planning, nuanced content? Opus. Worth every token.

The middle tier is where most teams waste money. They default everything to Sonnet because it feels "safe." But half those Sonnet calls are doing work Haiku handles identically, and the other half actually need Opus-level reasoning.

Beyond model selection, three things moved the needle:

Caching. If you're sending the same system prompt and context repeatedly, you're paying full price for tokens the API already processed. Prompt caching exists. Use it.

Context trimming. Most 200k token requests don't need 200k tokens. Summarize prior conversation. Strip irrelevant file contents. Send what matters.

Batching. If the response isn't time-sensitive, batch it. The price difference between sync and batch API calls is significant.

None of this requires switching providers. It requires treating inference like infrastructure instead of a magic black box.

remixes.label: cloud-bill-parallel
remixes.hook: We learned to optimize cloud bills in 2018. We're relearning the same lesson with LLMs in 2026.
remixes.body:
We learned to optimize cloud bills in 2018. We're relearning the same lesson with LLMs in 2026.

Remember when every startup was shocked by their first real AWS bill? Same containers running 24/7 for dev environments. No auto-scaling. Production databases sized for traffic they'd never hit. S3 buckets nobody cleaned up.

The fix wasn't "use less cloud." It was right-sizing, reserved instances, spot pricing, and actually understanding what you were paying for.

LLM costs are following the exact same curve. Teams are running the most expensive model on every call. Sending bloated contexts because nobody measured what the model actually needs. No caching. No tiering. No routing logic.

The playbook is identical:

Right-size your model per task. Haiku for extraction, Sonnet for synthesis, Opus for complex reasoning.

Reserve capacity. Prompt caching is the reserved instances of LLMs. Same input prefix, fraction of the cost.

Use spot pricing. Batch API endpoints give you 50% discounts for non-urgent work.

Clean up waste. Audit your token usage weekly. You'll find calls sending 10x the context needed.

The teams who figured out cloud cost optimization early had a structural advantage. The same thing is happening right now with inference costs.

posts.title: Agents replacing SDRs misses the point
posts.hook: "We replaced 6 SDRs with an agent" gets the likes. But it's the wrong frame.
posts.body:
"We replaced 6 SDRs with an agent" gets the likes. But it's the wrong frame.

The SDR job was never "send emails and book meetings." That's just what we reduced it to because the tooling was bad and the playbooks were lazy.

The actual job is figuring out who has a problem you solve, right now, and starting a conversation they want to have.

Agents are better at the mechanical parts. Enrichment, sequencing, list building, follow-up timing. A Python script with API access to Apollo, Exa, and an LLM can do in 90 seconds what used to take an SDR an afternoon.

But the interesting question isn't "how many SDRs can we cut." It's "what can those people do now that the mechanical work is automated?"

The best teams I'm seeing redeploy SDRs into signal research. They're the ones reading Reddit threads, joining Slack communities, spotting buying signals that no enrichment API surfaces. They're doing the work that requires taste, timing, and human judgment.

Automation doesn't replace people. It reveals whether the job was mechanical or creative. If the entire role was mechanical... yeah, an agent replaces it. But if you hire curious people and remove the grunt work, they become your best source of pipeline intelligence.
posts.cta: Curious what teams are actually doing with the time they're getting back from automation.

remixes.hook: The teams winning with AI sales agents didn't replace their SDRs. They made them dangerous.
remixes.body:
The teams winning with AI sales agents didn't replace their SDRs. They made them dangerous.

I keep seeing two camps. Camp one posts "we fired our SDR team and automated everything." Camp two says AI will never replace human sellers. Both are wrong.

The actual pattern that works: let agents handle the mechanical work that was always a bad use of human time. Signal monitoring. Data enrichment. Sequence personalization. Meeting scheduling. CRM hygiene.

Then take the humans who used to spend 6 hours a day on that grind and point them at the work machines can't do yet. Reading between the lines on a call. Noticing that a prospect's LinkedIn activity shifted from technical content to vendor evaluation. Crafting a message that references something only a human would catch.

One team I work with kept their two best SDRs and gave them agent-powered tooling. Those two now outperform the original team of eight. Not because the agents are doing the selling. Because the humans finally have time to do the actual selling instead of the busywork we mislabeled as selling.

The headcount reduction narrative makes for good LinkedIn engagement. But the teams quietly compounding results are playing the augmentation game.

remixes.label: job-definition-problem
remixes.hook: We didn't automate the SDR role. We automated the bad version of it we'd been running for a decade.
remixes.body:
We didn't automate the SDR role. We automated the bad version of it we'd been running for a decade.

Think about what most SDRs actually do day-to-day. Pull lists from ZoomInfo. Copy-paste into a sequence tool. Send templated emails with {{firstName}} personalization. Log activities in Salesforce. Follow up on auto-generated tasks. Hit activity metrics.

None of that is sales. That's data entry with a quota.

The actual SDR job, the one that creates pipeline, is pattern recognition. Who is showing buying signals right now? What specific problem are they trying to solve? What's the message that makes them stop scrolling?

Agents can absolutely handle the mechanical layer. Enrichment, sequencing, scheduling, data hygiene. They should. Humans were never good at it and hated doing it.

But when companies say "we replaced SDRs with agents," what they really mean is "we automated the assembly line we built because we didn't trust SDRs to think." The replacement wasn't AI vs. humans. It was admitting the job was designed wrong.

The interesting question isn't whether agents can replace SDRs. It's what the SDR role looks like when you strip away everything a machine does better.

When I advise teams on AI-driven sales automation, I consistently push back on the replacement framing. Here's why.

The SDR function was never meant to be "send emails and book meetings." That's what it devolved into because legacy tooling forced manual execution of tasks that should have been automated years ago.

The uncomfortable question nobody posting these "we replaced our SDRs" victory laps wants to answer: if your entire outbound motion can be replaced by an API call and a for loop, what does that say about the motion you were running?

The teams actually winning are using agents for the mechanical layer and redeploying humans to the strategic work. That's less viral but it's what actually builds pipeline.

posts.title: MCP is USB-C for AI tooling
posts.hook: MCP isn't exciting because of what it does today. It's exciting because of what it kills.
posts.body:
MCP isn't exciting because of what it does today. It's exciting because of what it kills.

Before MCP, connecting an AI agent to your tools meant writing custom integrations for every single one. Attio connector. Lemlist connector. PostHog connector. Each with its own auth flow, its own schema, its own edge cases.

Now I have MCP servers running for Attio, Lemlist, PostHog, Playwright, Typefully, and Exa. All connected to Claude Code through the same protocol. The agent sees all of them as available tools and picks the right one based on context.

Yesterday I asked Claude Code to check my campaign stats, pull the top-performing subject line, look up the company in my CRM, and draft a case study note. It chained four MCP tools without me specifying which ones. Just described what I needed.

This is what the "USB-C moment" actually means. Not that MCP is elegant (it is). Not that it's standardized (it is). But that it makes tool integration a commodity instead of a competitive moat.

The dev tools that adopt MCP become composable. The ones that don't become islands. And in a world where AI agents are the primary interface, being an island means being invisible.

I'm building my entire GTM stack as MCP-connectable components. The agent is the orchestrator. The tools are just... tools.

remixes.label: integration-graveyard
remixes.hook: I used to maintain 9 custom API integrations for my AI agent stack. Now I maintain zero.
remixes.body:
I used to maintain 9 custom API integrations for my AI agent stack. Now I maintain zero.

Every tool in my GTM workflow used to require its own connector. Attio needed a REST wrapper with OAuth. Lemlist had its own auth flow and weird pagination. PostHog required custom query builders. Playwright needed a browser management layer. Typefully had yet another API pattern.

Each integration was 200-400 lines of code. Each one broke whenever the vendor changed their API. Each one needed its own error handling, rate limiting, and schema validation.

posts.title: 2019 outbound is still everywhere
posts.hook: 500 emails a day with 0.1% reply rates isn't outbound. It's expensive noise.
posts.body:
500 emails a day with 0.1% reply rates isn't outbound. It's expensive noise.

I used to be the person sending volume. SDR at a startup, no tooling budget, just a spreadsheet and a primary domain with no warmup. I burned domains, hit spam folders, and learned the hard way that more volume with bad targeting just accelerates failure.

The playbook that works now is the opposite of what I ran in 2019.

Instead of 500 generic sends, it's 30 emails a day to people showing real buying signals. Job postings that match your use case. Funding rounds in your ICP. Reddit threads where someone describes the exact problem you solve. Tech stack changes visible in their site source.

The stack that makes this work:
- Exa or Google Alerts for signal detection
- Enrichment APIs (Apollo, PDL) for contact data
- SQLite for scoring and dedup
- Claude for personalization that actually references the signal
- Lemlist or Smartlead for sending infrastructure

Total cost per month... maybe $200-400 in API credits. No five-figure platform contract.

The teams still running 2019 playbooks aren't lazy. They just haven't seen what signal-led outbound looks like when you build the stack yourself. Once you see it, you can't go back to batch-and-blast.

The volume dropped from 500/day to maybe 30. The reply rate went from 0.1% to 12%. The pipeline impact went up, not down.

This isn't a secret. It's just harder than blasting volume, so most teams don't do it. You need signal infrastructure. You need enrichment that actually works. You need someone who can write a message that doesn't sound like a robot wrote it.

The 2019 playbook was volume. The 2026 playbook is timing.

The infrastructure is different. You need intent data, tech install monitoring, job posting scrapers, content engagement tracking. But the results aren't even comparable.

30 signal-led emails outperform 500 spray-and-pray emails every single time. I have the burned domains to prove the alternative doesn't work.

posts.title: Cut the team, rebuild the stack, double the pipeline
posts.hook: Cutting your SDR team in half only works if you rebuild the machine underneath them.
posts.body:
Cutting your SDR team in half only works if you rebuild the machine underneath them.

I see this pattern every month now. Team cuts headcount, pipeline drops, leadership panics, they rehire. The problem was never the people. It was that the system they worked inside was held together with Zaps and spreadsheets.

What actually works when you compress a team:

✅ Centralize your data layer. One source of truth for accounts, contacts, signals, and engagement. Not five tools with five different versions of the same company.

✅ Automate the research loop. Enrichment, scoring, and list building should run on a schedule, not when someone has a free afternoon.

✅ Build the content engine in parallel. Your remaining reps should be creating warm touches, not cold spraying. LinkedIn posts, community replies, async video.

✅ Instrument everything. If you can't see which signal led to which reply, you're guessing. Log the chain.

The teams doubling pipeline with fewer people aren't using magic tools. They're doing the boring infrastructure work that makes each person 3-4x more effective.

I built Clearbox because I lived this. The signal detection and routing layer that makes a small team competitive against a 10-person SDR floor... that's the real product.

remixes.label: systems-autopsy
remixes.hook: The layoffs didn't kill your pipeline. The duct tape did.
remixes.body:
The layoffs didn't kill your pipeline. The duct tape did.

Every team I've audited after a reduction has the same root cause. They cut people but kept the process. So now you have 3 reps doing the work of 6, using the same brittle Zapier chains and manual CSV uploads that barely worked at full capacity.

The pipeline didn't drop because you lost headcount. It dropped because your system had a 1:1 ratio of humans to workarounds, and you removed the humans.

What a proper rebuild looks like after cuts:

First, kill every manual handoff. If a rep is copying data between tools, that's a process failure, not a task. Automate it or delete it.

Second, collapse your tool stack. Most teams post-layoff are paying for 8 tools doing 3 jobs. Pick your source of truth and route everything through it.

Third, instrument what's left. You can't optimize a system you can't measure. Every stage needs a timestamp, a conversion rate, and an owner.

The companies that come out of reductions stronger aren't the ones who hire back faster. They're the ones who refuse to bolt new people onto old infrastructure.

remixes.label: counter-narrative
remixes.hook: Hot take: most teams should cut headcount. They just shouldn't do it the way they're doing it.
remixes.body:
Hot take: most teams should cut headcount. They just shouldn't do it the way they're doing it.

The typical playbook: revenue dips, board gets nervous, cut 40% of the SDR team, tell the survivors to "do more with less." Then pipeline craters and everyone acts surprised.

But the instinct to compress the team isn't wrong. Most sales orgs are overstaffed relative to their infrastructure. They hired people to compensate for broken systems instead of fixing the systems.

The right sequence matters:

1. Audit every rep's day. How many hours go to actual selling vs. data entry, tool switching, and list building? I've seen teams where reps spend 60% of their time on non-selling activities.

2. Automate the non-selling work first. Enrichment, routing, sequencing, CRM updates. Get that ratio to 80/20 before you touch headcount.

3. Then compress. Now each rep is genuinely 2x more productive, not just 2x more overworked.

4. Reinvest savings into the data and tooling layer that makes the smaller team sustainable.

The companies that skip steps 1 and 2 end up in the hire-fire-hire cycle. The ones that follow the sequence end up with a team that's smaller, faster, and less fragile.

posts.title: Content is outbound now
posts.hook: Your LinkedIn post is doing more pipeline work than your SDR sequences. Nobody wants to admit it.
posts.body:
Your LinkedIn post is doing more pipeline work than your SDR sequences. Nobody wants to admit it.

I track where my inbound comes from. Not vanity metrics. Actual conversations that turn into pipeline. And for the last 6 months, the breakdown looks like this:

- Cold email: ~15% of qualified conversations
- LinkedIn content + DMs: ~45%
- Reddit + community: ~30%
- Referrals: ~10%

The cold email still works. But it works because the person already saw my content somewhere else. The email is the last touch, not the first.

This isn't a "content marketing" strategy. It's a recognition that buyers research before they respond. They read your posts. They check your comment history. They look at whether you actually know what you're talking about or if you're just quoting a framework.

The practical implication: if you're a founder or GTM leader and you're not posting, you're invisible in the channels where your buyers actually spend time.

I post almost daily. Not because I love creating content. Because every post is a lightweight qualification filter. The people who resonate with the way I think about GTM are the same people who become good clients.

Content isn't a top-of-funnel play. It's a trust compression engine.

I tracked every qualified conversation for 6 months. Cold email came in last.

Not impressions. Not clicks. Actual humans who got on a call and had budget.

The breakdown:

LinkedIn content and DMs: 45% of qualified pipeline. A post gets traction, someone DMs, we talk. No sequence required. No "just following up" email #7.

Reddit and community: 30%. Answering real questions in niche subreddits. No selling. Just being useful in public. People check your profile, see you know what you're talking about, reach out.

Cold email: 15%. Still works for targeted, well-researched outreach. But the spray-and-pray era is dead. The messages that convert are the ones that reference something specific the prospect said or did publicly.

Referrals: 10%. The most qualified leads, but the least controllable channel.

The implication is uncomfortable for anyone running a traditional outbound motion. Your content IS your outbound now. Every post is a cold email that reaches thousands instead of dozens. Every comment is a warm intro that costs nothing.

The teams still pouring 80% of their budget into cold sequences are optimizing for a channel that produces 15% of the result. The math doesn't lie.

remixes.body:
Your SDR sequences are competing with content that already built trust before the first touchpoint.

Think about the last time you bought software. Did you respond to a cold email from someone you'd never heard of? Or did you already follow someone who talked about the problem, see their thinking, and reach out when you were ready?

The buying motion has inverted. Prospects now do 80% of their evaluation before they ever talk to sales. And where do they evaluate? LinkedIn feeds. Reddit threads. Community Slack channels. Newsletter archives.

posts.title: The GTM Engineer is the new 10x hire
posts.hook: Three years ago, "GTM Engineer" wasn't a job title. Now it's the hire that changes everything for small teams.
posts.body:
Three years ago, "GTM Engineer" wasn't a job title. Now it's the hire that changes everything for small teams.

A GTM engineer isn't a sales ops person who learned Python. And it's not a developer who read a sales book. It's someone who thinks in systems and builds the infrastructure that makes revenue repeatable.

What they actually do:
- Build enrichment pipelines that turn raw signals into scored accounts
- Wire up CRM automations that eliminate manual data entry
- Create dashboards that show pipeline health, not vanity metrics
- Connect tools via APIs and MCP instead of buying more point solutions
- Write the scripts that let 3 reps do the work of 10

The reason this role matters more at sub-50 person companies is simple. You can't afford specialized RevOps, Sales Ops, Marketing Ops, and Data Engineering. You need one person who covers all four and builds with code instead of buying with budget.

I became a GTM engineer by accident. I was a plumber who learned to code, then an SDR who got tired of manual workflows, then a founder who couldn't afford to hire separate ops roles. So I built the stack myself.

That's the profile. Someone who's been close enough to revenue to understand what matters, and technical enough to build it without waiting for engineering tickets.

Week 1-2: Audit the entire data flow. Map every tool, every integration, every manual step.

Week 3-6: Build the enrichment pipeline. Raw signals in, scored leads out. Automated, tested, monitored.

Week 7-10: Connect the CRM to reality. Bi-directional sync that actually works. No more "who updated this field?"

Week 11-12: Build the dashboard that shows what's working and what isn't. Real attribution, not last-touch nonsense.

This role didn't exist three years ago. Now it's the single highest-leverage hire for any team under 50 people.

posts.title: Claude agent replaced my market research workflow
posts.hook: Built a market research agent in a weekend. 6 hours of work now takes 25 minutes.
posts.body:
Built a market research agent in a weekend. 6 hours of work now takes 25 minutes.

The old workflow for researching a new market segment:
1. Google the space for 30 min
2. Find 10-15 companies manually
3. Check each website, pull positioning and pricing
4. Look up founders on LinkedIn
5. Search for funding data on Crunchbase
6. Check Reddit/X for user complaints and praise
7. Compile everything into a doc

The agent version:
1. Give it a market segment and ICP criteria
2. It runs Exa searches for companies matching the criteria
3. Enriches each with Apollo for contacts, org size, tech stack
4. Scrapes positioning from their websites via Playwright
5. Pulls Reddit mentions via public API
6. Scores and ranks them by fit
7. Outputs a structured SQLite database + summary doc

Same quality of research. Sometimes better, because the agent doesn't get bored on company #12 and start skimming.

The key insight wasn't the agent itself. It was realizing that market research is mostly structured data collection with a thin layer of judgment on top. The collection part is pure automation. The judgment part is where I spend my 25 minutes reviewing what the agent found.

Total cost per run: about $3-5 in API credits.

Here's the exact stack behind my market research agent. Total build time: one weekend.

I got tired of spending 6 hours on market research that followed the exact same pattern every time. Google the space. Find companies. Check websites. Look up founders. Pull funding data. Check community sentiment. Compile it into a doc nobody reads past page 2.

So I built an agent that does it in 25 minutes.

The stack: Claude as the reasoning layer. Exa for web search that actually understands semantic queries. A scraping layer for company websites and pricing pages. LinkedIn data enrichment for founder profiles. Crunchbase API for funding. Reddit and X APIs for community sentiment.

The workflow: I give it a market segment and 2-3 example companies. It finds 15-25 similar companies, pulls their positioning, pricing model, founding team, funding stage, and public sentiment. Then it generates a comparison matrix and a 1-page brief with the actual insight, not just raw data.

What surprised me: the agent catches things I would miss. It connects funding timing to product pivots. It spots positioning overlap between competitors I wouldn't have grouped together. It finds Reddit threads from 2 years ago where early users complained about exactly the gap I'm trying to fill.

The code is straightforward. The hard part was defining what "good research" looks like well enough to instruct an agent to do it. Once I nailed the prompt architecture, the rest was just API plumbing.

My market research agent paid for itself on the first run. Not in some abstract way. In actual hours I got back.

The math: I do market research for new segments about 3-4 times a month. Each one took roughly 6 hours. That's 18-24 hours of manual research monthly.

The agent does the same work in 25 minutes. Cost per run: about $0.80 in API calls.

Monthly savings: ~20 hours of my time. Monthly cost: ~$3.20 in API usage plus the weekend I spent building it.

But the real ROI isn't the time savings. It's what I do with those 20 hours. Instead of compiling data, I'm analyzing it. Instead of finding companies, I'm reaching out to them. Instead of reading Reddit threads, I'm building relationships in those communities.

The agent handles the parts that don't require judgment. Finding companies, pulling data, organizing information. I handle the parts that do. Spotting patterns, making strategic decisions, identifying opportunities the data alone doesn't reveal.

This is the framework I use for every automation decision: if the task is repeatable, structured, and doesn't require novel judgment, build the agent. If it requires taste, relationships, or strategic thinking, keep it human.

The 6-hour workflow wasn't hard. It was just tedious. And tedious work is exactly what agents are built for.

posts.title: Honest numbers beat highlight reels
posts.hook: Most build-in-public posts show the wins. The losses are where the lessons live.
posts.body:
Most build-in-public posts show the wins. The losses are where the lessons live.

Clearbox honest numbers from the last 30 days:
- 3 enterprise conversations that went cold after the second call
- 1 integration that broke in production because I didn't test the edge case
- A Reddit post I spent 2 hours writing that got 4 upvotes
- A LinkedIn post I wrote in 10 minutes that drove 3 inbound DMs

The pattern I keep seeing in my own data: effort and outcome have almost zero correlation in content. The posts where I overthink the structure and try to be clever... crickets. The posts where I share a specific thing I built or broke that day... conversations.

Same with sales. The prospects I chase hardest are the ones who ghost. The ones who find me through a post or a Reddit comment convert faster because they already self-selected.

Building in public isn't a marketing strategy. It's a forcing function for honesty. When you commit to sharing real numbers, you can't hide from the bad ones. And the bad ones are what actually make you adjust.

I'd rather have $2k MRR with 3 churned customers and a clear picture of why they left than $10k MRR with no idea what's working.

A Reddit post I spent 2 hours crafting got 4 upvotes. A LinkedIn post I wrote in 10 minutes drove 3 inbound DMs. The effort-to-outcome ratio in content is completely unpredictable, and anyone who tells you they've cracked the algorithm is selling something.

A pricing experiment lost me a qualified lead. I tested a higher tier, they balked, and by the time I adjusted they'd gone with a competitor. The data point was valuable. The deal was more valuable.

Why share this? Because the build-in-public posts that only show wins create a false picture. They make every other founder think they're the only one with a messy month. You're not. This is what building actually looks like. Wins and losses in roughly equal measure, with the lessons hiding in the losses.

I recommend every founder practice radical transparency with their numbers, at minimum with themselves, ideally with their audience.

Here's why: the build-in-public movement has a survivorship bias problem. The posts that get traction show hockey-stick growth, record months, and viral launches. This creates a distorted benchmark that makes normal building feel like failure.

My honest numbers from the last 30 days tell a different story. Three enterprise conversations went cold. An integration broke in production. A Reddit post I invested 2 hours in got minimal traction. A LinkedIn post I wrote in 10 minutes drove multiple inbound conversations.

What I recommend taking from this: first, effort and outcome are poorly correlated in content. Accept that and optimize for consistency over perfection. Second, enterprise deals stall for structural reasons, usually missing executive sponsors, not because your product isn't good enough. Third, production issues are inevitable. What matters is detection speed and recovery time, not prevention at all costs.

The practice of sharing honest numbers does two things. It forces you to actually look at what's working and what isn't, which is harder than it sounds when you're moving fast. And it builds trust with your audience in a way that curated highlight reels never will.

The most valuable insights in any business come from the losses, not the wins.

Notice how none of those have a neat takeaway? None of them end with "and that's when I realized the real treasure was the lessons I learned along the way." Some of them are just losses. They cost money and time and there's no silver lining.

The obsession with turning every failure into a growth narrative is its own form of dishonesty. Sometimes you just screwed up. Sometimes the month was bad. Sometimes the number is embarrassing.

Share those numbers. Not because it's a "strategy" or because vulnerability "builds trust." Share them because pretending everything is going well when it isn't is exhausting, and the people who've actually built something can smell the performance from a mile away.
